constitutive_assumptions: Dynamic memory and rate-dependent hysteresis: origami structures store and slowly release potential energy during deformation, making the current kinematic state dependent on historical actuation and deformation states
Quasi-static settling assumption: waiting 1 s after actuation and chamber pressurization allows the continuum structure to reach a quasi-static state for measurement
A 10-time-step sequential window is assumed sufficient to capture historical dependencies for long-term hysteresis modeling in the LSTM network

Constant curvature geometric approximation for tendon length compensation: neutral axis compression and segment bending are approximated via geometric trigonometric formulations to compensate for second-segment tendon slacking
Torsional deformation is assumed negligible during bending motions due to high structural torsional stiffness, supported by near-zero yaw angular deviations

Model-free data-driven kinematic assumption: hyper-redundant nonlinear structural deformations and manufacturing errors are mapped via neural network regression rather than explicit continuum mechanics constitutive laws
control_variables: Operating frequency of the control loop (50 Hz)
Pneumatic holding pressure for stiffness reinforcement and hysteresis mitigation (10 kPa applied for 2 s)
Quasi-static settling wait time before position acquisition (1 s)
Tendon pre-tensioning length reduction (8.45 mm for trajectory experiments; 7.53 mm in pre-tensioning characterization tests)
Window size of historical end-position time steps for LSTM input (10 time steps)
Initial training dataset size (4,800 random points)
Number of waypoints per evaluation trajectory (64 waypoints for standard curves; 32 waypoints for flower curves)
Neural network training duration (100 epochs, taking 228,436 ms)
Sensor sampling frequency of the motion capture system (50 Hz)
dependent_variables: End-position trajectory tracking error (Euclidean distance error in mm and relative error percentage over robot length)
Directional position errors along Cartesian axes (axial Z-axis error, lateral X- and Y-axis errors in mm)
Repeat positioning accuracy / repeatability error (Euclidean distance error in mm)
Bending orientation error / angular deviation (Euler angles: roll, pitch, and yaw in degrees)
Hysteresis displacement (origin position offset before and after compression cycles in mm)
Disturbance displacement of segment 1 caused by distal segment motion (mm)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Pre-tensioning the actuation tendons by 7.53 mm decreases compression hysteresis by 50% compared to an un-tensioned origami continuum module.
Pressurizing the internal origami chamber to 10 kPa accelerates hysteresis stabilization from 43 s to within 2 s and noticeably mitigates the accumulation of hysteresis.
Repeated positioning evaluation over 30 cycles across four spatial target points demonstrates an average repeat positioning accuracy of approximately 0.1 mm.
The dual origami architecture achieves an axial extension ratio of up to 110% through internal pneumatic chamber inflation.

Pressurization of the internal origami chamber causes radial expansion that eliminates the clearance gap between the inner and outer origami structures, providing layer-jamming friction that synergizes with tendon-pneumatic antagonistic forces to increase overall structural stiffness.

A stacked 2-layer LSTM network with an input window of 10 historical time steps trained iteratively on 4,800 points augmented with small step-size data achieves open-loop trajectory tracking errors of 1.58 mm (0.71% relative to length) for a single segment and 2.81 mm (0.63%) for multi-segments without sensory feedback.

The variable stiffness mechanism allows independent decoupled motion of the second segment while the first segment is locked in either a vertical or bent state, limiting disturbance displacements on the first segment to 1.06 mm and 0.86 mm, respectively.
Incorporating Euler angles into the LSTM training enables orientation control with an average angular deviation of 0.75 degrees (individual segment roll, pitch, and yaw errors under 1.4 degrees).

Carrying external payloads up to 240 g (twice the 120 g self-weight) results in tracking errors remaining around 3.69 mm (1.67%), with error growth concentrated predominantly in the axial Z direction.

The continuum robot executes open-loop multi-task demonstrations including drawing and letter writing ('ROBOT') on a 10-degree tilted board, board erasing, multi-segment simultaneous LED drawing ('USTC' and 'SOFT'), and pick-and-place manipulation of an 0.8 kg object using a suction cup.

experimental_setup: Dual origami continuum robot structure comprising an internal Miura crease sealed pneumatic chamber and an external Miura crease origami backbone with tendon routing holes
Seven-camera 3D optical motion capture system (Qualisys) operating at 50 Hz with +/-0.5 mm linear accuracy to track optical marker point clouds on the robot
Universal material testing machine executing cyclic compression tests (up to 50 cycles at 52.8 mm compression) for hysteresis quantification
Arduino Mega 2560 microcontroller communicating via CAN bus in daisy-chain configuration to drive tendon motors and via SPI bus to an analog DAC (TLV5610)
Pneumatic actuation circuit including an air pump, proportional pressure valve, solenoid valve, relay, and digital air pressure sensor regulating pressure at 10 kPa
Motor initial position monitoring using optocoupler sensors (MK012175)
Computing hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ CPU (2.8 GHz, 8 GB RAM) for control execution and NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU for PyTorch neural network training
Modular application tools: mounted writing brush, chalk eraser, optical LEDs for trajectory tracing, and vacuum suction cup for grasping a 0.8 kg load
future_work: Miniaturize and reduce the physical dimensions of the robot to develop collaborative devices for humans
Extend and apply the LSTM-based iterative training model to other continuum robotic structures
independent_variables: Actuation inputs: tendon length variations / motor displacements (0 to 44.38 mm effective range) and internal chamber pneumatic pressure (0 kPa, 10 kPa)
Tendon pre-tensioning displacement (0 mm vs. 7.53 mm / 8.45 mm)
Trajectory geometry and dimensions: shapes (astroid, circle, 8-shaped, flower, square, hexagon, sinusoidal), radii (10 mm to 60 mm), and central axial heights (-210 mm to -416 mm)
Operating motion velocity (low speed vs. high speed, up to 3.6x)
Applied external payload (0 g, 120 g, 240 g, and 0.8 kg manipulation target)
First segment structural state during second segment actuation (vertical high-stiffness state vs. bent high-stiffness state)
Iterative training cycle count (rounds 1 through 3) and dataset point composition (random points vs. random plus small step-size points)
Compression displacement levels during mechanical hysteresis testing (10.6, 21.1, 31.7, 42.3, and 52.8 mm) over 1 to 50 cycles
limitations_inferred: Data collection and trajectory evaluations rely on quasi-static holding phases (1 s wait time at waypoints), which restricts the dynamic bandwidth and real-time high-speed trajectory execution

Because control is completely open-loop without sensory feedback, unexpected external continuous contacts, variable environmental interactions, or long-term structural wear could induce uncompensated positioning drift
Manual origami fabrication processes may introduce manufacturing tolerances and structural discrepancies between distinct fabricated modules
Simultaneous multi-segment tracking exhibits larger tracking errors (5.90 mm, 1.34%) than isolated single-segment tracking, indicating residual inter-segment mechanical coupling and error compounding
Pneumatic actuation requires auxiliary support equipment (compressor/pump, proportional valves, solenoid valves, pressure sensors), limiting system untethered portability
limitations_stated_by_authors: Tracking error under load mainly arises from the axial direction (Z-axis error increases as payload increases), whereas no-load error primarily comes from lateral (X and Y) directions
Model prediction error plateaus after several iterative training rounds due to the influence of physical system factors
Movement of the first segment causes structural coupling that induces tendon slacking in the second segment, necessitating kinematic geometric compensation
Input window sizes below 10 time steps fail to capture sufficient historical information for accurate hysteresis modeling, while larger window sizes introduce computational overhead
Adding excessive neural network layers or neurons risks overfitting and escalates computational cost and training time
Robot hardware currently requires further integration and size reduction to develop human-collaborative devices
main_results: Achieved an average repeat positioning accuracy of approximately 0.1 mm across workspace target points over 30 cycles
Demonstrated that pre-tensioning reduced initial hysteresis by 50%, and applying 10 kPa pneumatic pressure reduced hysteresis stabilization time from >43 s to within 2 s

Single-segment open-loop trajectory tracking achieved an average Euclidean error of 1.58 mm (0.71% relative to robot length), with submillimeter tracking (<1 mm) on multiple trajectories (e.g., 0.93 mm on square, 0.72 mm on circle, 0.67 mm on 8-shaped)
Multi-segment tracking achieved an average trajectory tracking error of 2.81 mm (0.63% relative to length)
Demonstrated generalization to unlearned trajectory profiles, achieving 1.76 mm error (0.80%) on a single-segment hexagon and 1.04 mm error (0.23%) on a second-segment hexagon

Achieved independent motion decoupling of segment 2 under both vertical (1.07 mm error, 0.24%) and bent (3.28 mm error, 0.74%) locked states of segment 1, with segment 1 disturbance errors held to 1.06 mm and 0.86 mm
Simultaneous multi-segment trajectory tracking yielded an average position error of 5.90 mm (1.34% relative error)

Orientation control achieved an overall average angle error of 0.75 degrees (segment 1 roll/pitch/yaw: 0.99/1.06/0.22 degrees; segment 2 roll/pitch/yaw: 0.90/0.99/0.24 degrees; dynamic sinusoidal trajectory errors: 0.83/1.39/0.19 degrees)

Under payload increases up to 240 g (2x self-weight), tracking error increased by a factor of 2.64 to ~3.69 mm (1.67%), and speed increases up to 3.6x maintained errors within 1.23% relative to length
Successfully demonstrated open-loop sensorless task execution: precision writing and erasing on a 10-degree tilted board, multi-segment LED pattern drawing, and grasping/transferring an 0.8 kg object
modeling_methods: Stacked 2-layer Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) recurrent neural network for inverse kinematic modeling with hysteresis compensation
Iterative learning strategy augmenting limited random point datasets with actual trajectory execution and small step-size data
Neural network-based search optimizer and coordinate transformation for multi-segment inverse kinematic solutions
Analytical tendon compensation model based on constant-curvature neutral axis compression to eliminate second-segment tendon slacking
Euler angle orientation mapping via LSTM network for 3D spatial orientation control
performance_metrics: Trajectory tracking Euclidean distance error (absolute in mm and relative error percentage over robot length)
Directional Cartesian error components (axial Z error vs. lateral X and Y errors in mm)
Repeat positioning accuracy (Euclidean distance error in mm over 30 cycles)
Bending orientation error (absolute deviation in degrees for roll, pitch, and yaw Euler angles)
Mechanical hysteresis displacement (mm) and settling time (seconds)
Payload tracking error degradation factor relative to no-load conditions
Neural network training convergence time (milliseconds for 100 epochs)
possible_gap_implications: While open-loop model-free control eliminates vulnerability to sensor failure in harsh environments such as nuclear radiation, its reliance on pre-calibrated quasi-static hysteresis mapping implies potential vulnerability to unmodeled dynamic contact forces or gradual material degradation over extended deployment

The combination of pneumatic layer jamming and antagonistic tendon forces successfully circumvents the trade-off between compliance and load capacity, yet reliance on active pneumatic supply lines may hinder miniaturization or completely untethered field applications

Demonstrated transferability of single-segment kinematic learning to multi-segment configurations suggests that modular data-driven modeling can reduce calibration burdens in hyper-redundant continuum robots, provided mechanical coupling and tendon slacking can be geometrically compensated
paper.research_objective: To develop a novel design and learning-based control scheme for a rear-driven multi-segment hybrid-actuated soft origami continuum robot that achieves decoupled segment motion and submillimeter/millimeter-level trajectory tracking accuracy without sensory feedback, employing a dual-origami hybrid variable stiffness mechanism (antagonistic actuation and layer jamming) and an LSTM-based iterative learning framework that compensates for origami hysteresis.
paper.research_problem: Soft origami continuum robots have infinite degrees of freedom, high compliance, and adaptability, but suffer from low control accuracy, limited load-carrying capacity, motion coupling among segments in rear-driven multi-segment architectures with high extension ratios, rate-dependent saturated hysteresis, and vulnerability to sensor failure in harsh environments (e.g., nuclear radiation) where conventional closed-loop electronic feedback cannot function.
paper.robot_type: multi-segment hybrid-actuated soft origami continuum robot
paper.title: Decoupling Control of a Multi-Segment Hybrid-Actuated Soft Origami Continuum Robot Through Variable Stiffness
